source: 時，婆羅門即作是念：「過去世中有無量恒河沙等諸佛世尊，我曾不習近。設復未來如無量恒河沙三藐三佛陀，亦當不與習近娛樂。我今當於沙門瞿曇所修行梵行。」即便合掌白佛言：「唯願聽我於正法、律出家修梵行。」
A:
At that time, the Brahmin thought to himself: "In the past, there were Buddhas and Blessed Ones (buddha bhagavant) as numerous as the sands of the Ganges (gaṅgā-nadī-vālukā), yet I never drew near to them. Even if in the future there are as many perfectly enlightened ones (samyak-saṃbuddha) as the sands of the Ganges, I shall not draw near to them or find delight in them either. Now, I shall cultivate the holy life (brahmacarya) under the recluse Gotama (śramaṇa gautama)."

He then pressed his palms together and said to the Buddha: "I only wish that you would allow me to go forth (pravrajyā) into the right Dharma (saddharma) and discipline to cultivate the holy life."
B: At that time, the brāhmaṇa (brāhmaṇa) thought to himself: "In the past there were Buddhas, Blessed Ones (buddha bhagavant) as numerous as the sands of the Ganges (gaṅgā-nadī-vālukā), yet I did not attend upon them. Even if in the future there are fully and perfectly awakened ones (samyaksambuddha) as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, I will likewise not attend upon them or find delight in them. I shall now cultivate the holy life (brahmacarya) under the recluse Gautama (śramaṇa gautama)." He then joined his palms together and said (ah) to the Buddha: "I only wish that you would allow me to go forth (pravraj) in the right Dharma (dharma) and discipline to cultivate the holy life."

source: 佛告須菩提：「色如相，受、想、行、識如相，乃至涅槃如相，是阿耨多羅三藐三菩提。是如相亦不增不減。須菩提！是菩薩摩訶薩不離般若波羅蜜，常觀是如法，不見有增有減。以是因緣故，須菩提！不可說義無增無減，檀波羅蜜亦不增不減，乃至十八不共法亦不增不減。須菩提！菩薩摩訶薩以是不增不減法故，應般若波羅蜜行。」
A:
The Buddha said to Subhūti, "Form is the nature of suchness (tathatā), and feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are the nature of suchness, up to and including nirvāṇa, which is the nature of suchness. This is the unsurpassed, perfect awakening (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi). This nature of suchness neither increases nor decreases.

Subhūti, this bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not depart from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā); he constantly contemplates this dharma of suchness and does not perceive any increase or decrease. For this reason, Subhūti, the inexpressible (anabhilāpya) meaning is without increase or decrease; the perfection of generosity (dāna-pāramitā) also neither increases nor decreases, up to and including the eighteen exclusive qualities of a Buddha (aṣṭādaśāveṇikabuddhadharma), which also neither increase nor decrease.

Subhūti, because of this dharma of non-increase and non-decrease, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva should practice the perfection of wisdom."
B: The Buddha said to Subhūti: "The form is the nature of suchness (tathatā), and feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are the nature of suchness, up to and including the nature of suchness of nirvāṇa; this is the unexcelled perfect awakening (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi). This nature of suchness neither increases nor decreases. Subhūti, this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva does not depart from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), constantly contemplating this dharma of suchness, and does not perceive any increase or decrease. Because of this causal condition (pratyaya), Subhūti, the inexpressible (anabhilāpya) meaning neither increases nor decreases; the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā) also neither increases nor decreases, up to and including the eighteen exclusive qualities (āveṇika-dharma) which also neither increase nor decrease. Subhūti, because of this dharma of non-increase and non-decrease, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should practice the perfection of wisdom."

source: 復次，無想等至，當言唯一有漏。滅盡等至當言無漏。由與煩惱不相應故、非相應故、無所緣故、非諸煩惱之所生故。是出世間，一切異生不能行故。唯除已入遠地菩薩。菩薩雖能起出世法，令現在前，然由方便善巧力故，不捨煩惱。又此等至，當言非學非無學攝，非所行故，似涅槃故。
A: Furthermore, the attainment of non-perception (asaṃjñā-samāpatti) should be described as exclusively tainted (āsrava). The attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) should be described as untainted (anāsrava), because it is not associated with afflictions (kleśa), is not connected to them, has no object of perception, and is not produced by any afflictions. It is supramundane (lokottara), as it cannot be practiced by any ordinary person (pṛthagjana). The only exception is a bodhisattva who has entered the distant stage (dūraṃgamā-bhūmi). Although a bodhisattva is able to manifest supramundane phenomena, through the power of skillful means (upāya-kauśalya), they do not abandon the afflictions. Moreover, this attainment should be described as being included neither in the category of the learner nor the non-learner, because it is not a sphere of activity and resembles nirvana (nirvāṇa).
B: Furthermore, the attainment of non-perception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) should be spoken of as exclusively tainted (sāsrava). The attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) should be spoken of as untainted (anāsrava), because it is not associated with the afflictions (kleśa), because it is not connected to them, because it has no object of perception (ālambana), and because it is not produced by any of the afflictions. It is supramundane (lokottara), because all ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) are unable to practice it, with the sole exception of those bodhisattvas who have entered the distant stages. Although a bodhisattva is able to manifest supramundane phenomena (lokottara-dharma), through the power of skillful means (upāya-kauśalya) they do not abandon the afflictions. Moreover, this attainment should be spoken of as included in the category of neither a learner nor a non-learner (naivaśaikṣa-anāśaikṣa), because it is not an object of practice and because it resembles nirvana (nirvāṇa).

source: 論曰：由田勝者，聞有苾芻於僧眾中作女人語，彼於現世轉作女人。此等傳聞其類非一。由意勝者，聞有黃門救脫諸牛黃門事故，彼於現世轉作丈夫。此等傳聞事亦非一。或生此地永離此地染，於此地中諸善不善業。於異熟定位不定者，此業必能招現法果。若有餘位順定受業，彼必定無永離染義，必於餘位受異熟果。若於異熟亦不定者，永離染故不受異熟。何田起業定即受耶？頌曰：
A:
The treatise says: Regarding those superior in terms of the field, it is heard that a bhikṣu (monk) spoke to the community of monks using the speech of a woman, and in this very lifetime he was transformed into a woman. Such reports are not singular. Regarding those superior in terms of intention, it is heard that a eunuch (paṇḍaka) saved some cattle from a eunuch-related incident, and in this very lifetime he was transformed into a man (puruṣa). Such reports are also not singular.

As for wholesome and unwholesome karman (action) performed in this state, if one is born into this state and permanently detaches from the defilements (vairāgya) of this state, then for that karman which is uncertain regarding the timing of its ripening (vipāka), that karman will inevitably bring about a result in the present lifetime (dṛṣṭadharma). If there is other karman that is certain to be experienced in a subsequent state, then for that person there is no meaning in having permanently detached from defilements, for they will certainly experience the ripening in a subsequent state. If the ripening itself is also uncertain, then because one has permanently detached from defilements, one will not experience the ripening.

What is the field from which karman arises such that it is certain to be experienced? The gāthā (verse) says:
B:
The treatise says: Regarding the excellence of the field, it is heard that there was a monk (bhikṣu) who spoke with the voice of a woman among the community of monks, and because of that, he was transformed into a woman in this very lifetime (dṛṣṭadharma). Such accounts are not singular. Regarding the excellence of intention, it is heard that there was a eunuch who saved cattle from the affairs of eunuchs, and because of that, he was transformed into a man (puruṣa) in this very lifetime. Such accounts are also not singular.

Whether one is born in this realm or has permanently detached from the defilements (vairāgya) of this realm, regarding the wholesome and unwholesome actions (akuśala-karman) performed in this realm: if the ripening (vipāka) is certain but the timing is uncertain, this action will inevitably bring about a result in the present life. If there is an action that is certain to be experienced in another lifetime, then for that person, there is no possibility of permanent detachment from defilements; they will certainly experience the ripening of the result in another lifetime. If the ripening itself is also uncertain, then because one has permanently detached from defilements, one will not experience the ripening. 

From what field does an action arise such that it is certain to be experienced? The verse says:

source: 善男子！我亦依法無我性所顯勝義無自性性，密意說言一切諸法無生無滅、本來寂靜、自性涅槃。何以故？法無我性所顯勝義無自性性，於常常時、於恒恒時，諸法法性安住無為，一切雜染不相應故；於常常時、於恒恒時，諸法法性安住故無為。由無為故，無生無滅；一切雜染不相應故，本來寂靜、自性涅槃。是故我依法無我性所顯勝義無自性性，密意說言一切諸法無生無滅、本來寂靜、自性涅槃。
A:
"Good son, based on the ultimate nature of non-essence (paramārtha-niḥsvabhāva-tā) manifested through the nature of the non-self of phenomena (dharma-nairātmya), I have spoken with hidden intent (abhisandhāya) that all phenomena (sarva-dharma) are without arising (anutpāda), without cessation (anirodha), originally quiescent (prakṛti-praśānta), and by nature in nirvana (svabhāva-nirvāṇa).

Why is this? Because the ultimate nature of non-essence, manifested through the nature of the non-self of phenomena, remains at all times and in all periods established as the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) nature of phenomena (dharmatā), being dissociated from all defilements (saṃkleśa). Because it remains established as the nature of phenomena at all times and in all periods, it is unconditioned. Because it is unconditioned, it is without arising and without cessation; and because it is dissociated from all defilements, it is originally quiescent and by nature in nirvana. Therefore, based on the ultimate nature of non-essence manifested through the nature of the non-self of phenomena, I have spoken with hidden intent that all phenomena are without arising, without cessation, originally quiescent, and by nature in nirvana."
B: "Good son (kula-putra)! Based on the ultimate nature of non-essence (paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā) manifested by the nature of the non-self of phenomena (dharma-nairātmya), I have spoken with hidden intent (abhisandhāya) that all phenomena (sarva-dharma) are without birth, without cessation, originally quiescent (ādi-śānta), and by nature in nirvana (prakṛti-parinirvṛta). Why is this? Because the ultimate nature of non-essence manifested by the nature of the non-self of phenomena is, at all times and at all moments, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) abiding in the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), being dissociated (viprayukta) from all defilements; because at all times and at all moments, the nature of phenomena abides, it is therefore unconditioned. Because it is unconditioned, there is no birth and no cessation; because it is dissociated from all defilements, it is originally quiescent and by nature in nirvana. Therefore, based on the ultimate nature of non-essence manifested by the nature of the non-self of phenomena, I have spoken with hidden intent that all phenomena are without birth, without cessation, originally quiescent, and by nature in nirvana."

source: 云何菩薩善士精進？謂此精進略有五種。一、無所棄捨精進。謂諸菩薩所有精進，不捨一切欲加行故。二、無退減精進。謂諸菩薩所有精進，如先所受若等若增，發勤精進隨長養故。三、無下劣精進。謂諸菩薩所有精進，勇猛、熾然、長時、無間精勤策勵，心無怯弱、無退屈故。四、無顛倒精進。謂諸菩薩所有精進，能引義利，方便善巧所攝持故。五、勤勇加行精進。謂諸菩薩所有精進，能於無上正等菩提達進趣故。
A:
How does the bodhisattva (bodhisattva) possess the excellence of exertion (vīrya)? In brief, this exertion is of five kinds.

First, the exertion of non-abandonment. This means that the bodhisattva’s exertion does not abandon the application to all desires (sarva-kāma).

Second, the exertion of non-diminishment. This means that the bodhisattva’s exertion, whether equal to or greater than what was previously received (pūrva-anubhū), is cultivated and nurtured by initiating exertion (ārabh-vīrya).

Third, the exertion of non-inferiority. This means that the bodhisattva’s exertion is courageous, ardent, long-lasting, and uninterrupted (ānantarya), with a mind that is neither timid nor discouraged.

Fourth, the exertion of non-perversion (aviparīta). This means that the bodhisattva’s exertion is able to lead to benefit and is held by skillful means (upāya-kauśalya).

Fifth, the exertion of diligent application. This means that the bodhisattva’s exertion is able to advance toward the unsurpassed, perfect awakening (anuttara-samyaksambodhi).
B:
What is the exertion (vīrya) of a bodhisattva? In brief, this exertion consists of five types.

First, the exertion of non-abandonment. This means that the bodhisattva does not abandon any of the preparatory efforts (prayoga) he has undertaken.

Second, the exertion of non-diminishment. This means that the bodhisattva’s exertion is such that he maintains or increases what he has previously undertaken, diligently cultivating and nurturing it.

Third, the exertion of non-inferiority (avara). This means that the bodhisattva’s exertion is courageous, intense, long-term (dīrgha-kāla), and continuous (ānantarya), with a mind that is neither timid nor discouraged.

Fourth, the exertion of non-perversion. This means that the bodhisattva’s exertion is guided and supported by skillful means (upāya-kauśalya) that lead to true benefit (artha).

Fifth, the exertion of diligent application. This means that the bodhisattva’s exertion is capable of advancing him toward supreme, perfect awakening (anuttara-samyaksambodhi).

source: 「若諸善法生，一切皆明為根本，明集、明生、明起。明，於善、不善法如實知者，罪、無罪，親近、不親近，卑法、勝法，穢污、白淨，有分別、無分別，緣起、非緣起悉如實知，如實知者，是則正見。正見者，能起正志、正語、正業、正命、正方便、正念、正定。正定起已，聖弟子得正解脫貪、恚、癡，貪、恚、癡解脫已，是聖弟子得正智見：『我生已盡，梵行已立，所作已作，自知不受後有。』」
A: “If any wholesome states (kuśala-dharma) arise, all of them have clarity (vidyā) as their root, clarity as their gathering, clarity as their arising, and clarity as their manifestation. Clarity is the knowing things as they really are (yathābhūtam prajñā) regarding wholesome and unwholesome states (akuśala-dharma): knowing as they really are what is blameworthy and blameless, what should be cultivated and what should not be cultivated, what is base and what is superior, what is defiled and what is pure, what is with conceptualization (vikalpa) and what is without conceptualization (nirvikalpa), and what is dependently originated and what is not dependently originated. Knowing things as they really are is right view. Through right view, one is able to give rise to right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort (upāya), right mindfulness, and right concentration. Once right concentration has arisen, the noble disciple (ārya-śrāvaka) attains right liberation (vimokṣa) from greed, hatred, and delusion. Once liberated from greed, hatred, and delusion, this noble disciple attains right knowledge and vision: ‘Birth for me has been eradicated, the holy life (brahmacarya) has been established, what had to be done (kṛtya) has been done, I myself know that there will be no receiving of any further existence.’”
B:
“When any wholesome states arise, clarity (vidyā) is their root, their gathering, their origin, and their source. Clarity is the knowledge of wholesome and unwholesome states as they truly are: of what is blameworthy and blameless, what should be cultivated and what should not, what is base and what is superior, what is defiled and what is pure, what involves conceptual proliferation (vikalpa) and what is free from it (nirvikalpa), and what is dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) and what is not. To know these things as they truly are is right view (samyagdṛṣṭi).

From right view, one is able to give rise to right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort (upāya), right mindfulness (smṛti), and right concentration. Once right concentration has arisen, the noble disciple attains right liberation (vimukti) from greed, hatred, and delusion. Once liberated from greed, hatred, and delusion, this noble disciple attains right knowledge and vision: ‘Birth for me has been eradicated, the holy life (brahmacarya) has been established, what had to be done (kṛtya) has been done, and I know for myself that there will be no receiving of any further existence.’”

source: 云何漸次悟入唯識？謂諸菩薩於識相、性，資糧位中能深信解；在加行位能漸伏除所取、能取，引發真見；在通達位如實通達；修習位中如所見理，數數修習伏斷餘障；至究竟位出障圓明，能盡未來化有情類，復令悟入唯識相、性。
A: How does one gradually awaken to and enter Consciousness-Only (vijñaptimātra)? It is said that Bodhisattvas, during the stage of provisioning (sambhāra-bhūmi), are able to deeply believe in and understand the characteristics (lakṣaṇa) and nature (svabhāva) of consciousness. During the stage of applied effort (prayoga-bhūmi), they are able to gradually subdue and eliminate the grasped (grāhya) and the grasper (grāhaka), thereby inducing true vision (yathābhūta-darśana). During the stage of realization (prativedha-bhūmi), they realize these truths as they truly are. During the stage of cultivation (bhāvanā-bhūmi), they repeatedly practice in accordance with the principles they have perceived, so as to subdue and sever the remaining hindrances. Upon arriving at the ultimate stage (niṣṭhā-bhūmi), they emerge from all obstacles with perfect clarity, able to transform all classes of sentient beings until the end of time (anāgata), and in turn, cause them to awaken to and enter the characteristics and nature of Consciousness-Only.
B: How does one gradually awaken to and enter Consciousness-Only (vijñapti-mātra)? It means that Bodhisattvas, during the stage of provisioning (sambhāra), are able to deeply believe in and understand the characteristics (lakṣaṇa) and nature (svabhāva) of consciousness; during the stage of applied effort (prayoga), they are able to gradually subdue and eliminate the grasped (grāhya) and the grasper (grāhaka) to induce true vision (darśana); during the stage of realization (pratipatti), they realize these as they truly are (yathābhūtam); during the stage of cultivation (bhāvanā), they repeatedly practice in accordance with the principles they have perceived to subdue and sever the remaining hindrances; and upon arriving at the ultimate stage (niṣṭhā), they emerge from obstacles with perfect clarity, able to transform all classes of sentient beings (sattva-nikāya) until the end of time (anāgata), and cause them to awaken to and enter the characteristics and nature of Consciousness-Only.

source: 論曰：善無漏法亦名為妙。諸染污法亦名有罪有覆及劣。准此妙劣，餘中已成，故頌不辯。諸有為善亦名應習，餘非應習義准已成。何故無為不名應習？不可數習令增長故。又習為果，此無果故。解脫涅槃亦名無上，以無一法能勝涅槃，是善是常超眾法故。餘法有上，義准已成。
A: The treatise states: Virtuous, undefiled phenomena (anāsrava-dharma) are also called "excellent" (śubha/kalyāṇa). All defiled phenomena (kliṣṭa-dharma) are also called "faulty," "veiled," and "inferior." Based on these categories of excellent and inferior, the status of the remaining phenomena is already established by implication, and therefore the verse does not discuss them. All virtuous conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma) are also called "to be cultivated," while the opposite is established by implication as not to be cultivated. Why is the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) not called "to be cultivated"? Because it cannot be repeatedly practiced to bring about growth. Furthermore, cultivation aims at a result, and this has no result. Liberation (vimokṣa) and Nirvana (nirvāṇa) are also called "unsurpassed" (anuttara), because no single phenomenon can surpass Nirvana, as it is virtuous, eternal (nitya), and transcends all phenomena. That other phenomena are "surpassed" is established by implication.
B: The treatise says: Virtuous undefiled phenomena (anāsrava-dharma) are also called excellent (anuttara). All defiled phenomena (kliṣṭa) are also called faulty, covered, and inferior. Based on these categories of excellent and inferior, the status of the remainder is already established by implication, and therefore the verse does not discuss it. All virtuous conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta) are also called worthy of cultivation; the remainder is not worthy of cultivation, which is established by implication. Why is the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) not called worthy of cultivation? Because it cannot be repeatedly cultivated to cause growth. Furthermore, cultivation has a result, and this has no result. Liberation (vimukti) and Nirvana (nirvāṇa) are also called supreme (anuttara), because there is not one phenomenon that can surpass Nirvana, as it is virtuous, eternal, and transcends all phenomena. The remainder of phenomena have something superior to them, which is established by implication.

source: 佛言：「不與不善法合，不與善法合；不與世間法合，不與出世間法合；不與有漏法合，不與無漏法合；不與有罪法合，不與無罪法合；不與有為法合，不與無為法合。何以故？般若波羅蜜不為得諸法故生，以是故於諸法無所合。」
A: The Buddha said: "It does not combine with unwholesome phenomena (akuśala-dharma), nor does it combine with wholesome phenomena (kuśala-dharma); it does not combine with worldly phenomena (laukika-dharma), nor does it combine with supramundane phenomena (lokottara-dharma); it does not combine with phenomena subject to influxes (āsrava-dharma), nor does it combine with phenomena free from influxes (anāsrava-dharma); it does not combine with faulty phenomena (anavadya-dharma), nor does it combine with faultless phenomena (anavadya-dharma); it does not combine with conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma), nor does it combine with unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma). Why is this? The perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) does not arise for the sake of attaining phenomena (dharma); for this reason, it has no combination with any phenomena."
B: The Buddha said: "It does not combine with unwholesome phenomena (akuśala-dharma), nor does it combine with wholesome phenomena (kuśala-dharma). It does not combine with worldly phenomena (loka), nor does it combine with supramundane phenomena. It does not combine with phenomena subject to influxes (āsrava), nor does it combine with phenomena free from influxes (anāsrava-dharma). It does not combine with faulty phenomena, nor does it combine with faultless phenomena (anavadya). It does not combine with conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma), nor does it combine with unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma). Why is this? The perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) does not arise for the sake of attaining any phenomena; for this reason, it does not combine with any phenomena."

source: 答：當正了知唯有其名、唯遍計執，無相、無性、無生、無滅、無染、無淨，本來寂靜、自性涅槃，非過去、非未來、非現在，非繫、非離繫，非縛、非解脫，非苦、非樂、非不苦不樂，唯是一味，遍一切處皆如虛空。以如是等無量行相，應正了知遍計所執自性。
A: Response: One should correctly understand that it is merely a name, merely an imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva), without characteristics (animitta), without intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva), without arising (anutpāda), without cessation, without defilement, without purification. It is originally tranquil, by its own nature a state of liberation (nirvāṇa), neither of the past, nor of the future, nor of the present. It is neither bound nor liberated from bonds, neither tied nor released, neither suffering, nor pleasant, nor neutral. It is of a single flavor, and in all places (sarvatra) it is like space (ākāśa). Through these and other immeasurable aspects (ākāra), one should correctly understand the imagined nature.
B: Response: One should correctly understand that there is only a name, only the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva), without characteristics, without intrinsic nature (svabhāva), without arising, without ceasing, without defilement, without purification, originally tranquil (ādi-śānta), and naturally liberated (prakṛti-parinirvṛta). It is not of the past, not of the future, not of the present; it is not bound, not released from bonds; it is not tied, not liberated (vimokṣa); it is not suffering, not pleasant, not neither-suffering-nor-pleasant (aduḥkha-asukha). It is only of one flavor, and everywhere (sarvatra) it is like space (ākāśa). By means of these and other such immeasurable aspects, one should correctly understand the imagined nature.

source: 佛告須菩提：「三千大千世界中諸惡魔皆愁毒，如箭入心，各於其坐不能自安。須菩提！菩薩摩訶薩能如是行般若波羅蜜，是時一切世間天及人、阿修羅不能得其便令其憂惱。須菩提！以是故，菩薩摩訶薩欲得阿耨多羅三藐三菩提，當行是般若波羅蜜！菩薩摩訶薩行般若波羅蜜時，具足修檀波羅蜜、尸羅波羅蜜、羼提波羅蜜、毘梨耶波羅蜜、禪波羅蜜、般若波羅蜜。須菩提！菩薩摩訶薩行般若波羅蜜時，具足諸波羅蜜。」
A:
The Blessed One said to Subhūti, "Within the three-thousand-fold great thousand-world system, all the evil demons (māra) are filled with sorrow and poison, as if pierced by an arrow in the heart, and each is unable to remain at ease in his seat. Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva (great being) practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) in this way, at that time, all the gods, humans, and asuras (demigods) of the world cannot find an opportunity to cause him distress or anxiety.

Subhūti, for this reason, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to attain the unsurpassed, perfect awakening (anuttara-samyaksambodhi) should practice this perfection of wisdom. When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he fully cultivates the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā), the perfection of morality (śīlapāramitā), the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā), the perfection of effort (vīryapāramitā), the perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā), and the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he fulfills all the perfections."
B: The Buddha said to Subhūti, "In the three-thousand-fold great thousand-fold world system (tri-sāhasra-mahat-sāhasra-lokadhātu), all the evil demons are sorrowful and pained, as if an arrow had entered their hearts, and each is unable to remain at ease in his seat. Subhūti, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva (great being) can practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā) in this way, at that time all the gods, humans, and antigods (asura) in the entire world (sarva-loka) cannot find an opportunity to cause him worry or affliction. Subhūti, for this reason, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who wishes to attain unsurpassed, perfect awakening (anuttara-samyaksambodhi) should practice this perfection of wisdom. When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he fully cultivates the perfection of generosity (dāna-pāramitā), the perfection of morality (śīla-pāramitā), the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), the perfection of effort (vīrya-pāramitā), the perfection of meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā), and the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he fully possesses all the perfections (sarva-pāramitā)."

source: 爾時，世尊告諸比丘：「轉輪王七寶具足，成就人中四種神力，王四天下，身壞命終，生於天上。雖復轉輪聖王七寶具足，成就人間神力，王四天下，身壞命終，得生天上，然猶未斷地獄、畜生、餓鬼惡趣之苦。所以者何？以轉輪王不得於佛不壞淨，法、僧不壞淨，聖戒不成就故。
A: At that time, the Blessed One (bhagavant) addressed the monks (bhikṣu): "The Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin) is endowed with the seven treasures (saptan-ratna) and possesses the four kinds (caturvidha) of human power. He rules over the four continents (catur-dvīpa), and upon the breaking up of the body after death, he is reborn in the heavenly world. Although the noble Wheel-Turning King is endowed with the seven treasures, possesses human power, rules over the four continents, and upon the breaking up of the body after death attains rebirth in the heavenly world, he has not yet cut off the suffering of the hells (naraka), the animal realm, and the hungry ghosts (preta)—the states of woe (apāya). For what reason? Because the Wheel-Turning King has not attained the unwavering purity in the Buddha, the unwavering purity in the Dharma and the Saṅgha, and has not perfected the noble moral discipline (śikṣāpada)."
B: At that time, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "A Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin) is endowed with the seven treasures and possesses the four kinds of human power. He rules over the four continents, and upon the breaking up of his body after death, he is reborn in the heavenly realms. Although a Noble Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin-rājan) is endowed with the seven treasures, possesses human power, rules over the four continents, and upon the breaking up of his body after death is reborn in the heavenly realms, he has not yet cut off the suffering of the hells (naraka), the animal realm (tiryañc), and the realm of hungry ghosts (preta)—the states of woe (apāya). Why is this? Because the Wheel-Turning King has not attained the unwavering confidence in the Buddha, the unwavering confidence in the Dharma and the Sangha, nor has he perfected the noble morality (śīla)."

source: 佛告須菩提：「信般若波羅蜜，則不信色，不信受、想、行、識；不信眼乃至意；不信色乃至法；不信眼界乃至意識界；不信檀波羅蜜、尸羅波羅蜜、羼提波羅蜜、毘梨耶波羅蜜、禪波羅蜜；不信內空乃至無法有法空；不信四念處乃至八聖道分；不信佛十力乃至十八不共法；不信須陀洹果、斯陀含果、阿那含果、阿羅漢果、辟支佛道；不信菩薩道；不信阿耨多羅三藐三菩提乃至一切種智。」
A: The Buddha said to Subhūti: "To believe in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is to not believe in form (rūpa), to not believe in feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), volitional formations (saṃskāra), and consciousness (vijñāna); to not believe in the eye up to the mind; to not believe in visible objects up to phenomena (dharma); to not believe in the eye-element up to the mind-consciousness element; to not believe in the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā), the perfection of moral discipline (śīlapāramitā), the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā), the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā), and the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā); to not believe in internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the existence and non-existence of phenomena; to not believe in the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; to not believe in the ten powers of a Buddha up to the eighteen special attributes; to not believe in the fruit of a stream-enterer (srotaāpatti-phala), the fruit of a once-returner, the fruit of a non-returner (anāgāmin-phala), the fruit of an arhat (arhant-phala), and the path of a solitary buddha; to not believe in the path of a bodhisattva; to not believe in unsurpassed, perfect awakening (samyaksambodhi) up to the omniscience of all aspects (sarva-ākārajña)."
B: The Buddha said to Subhūti: "To have faith in the Perfection of Wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is to have no faith in form (rūpa), nor in feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), mental formations (saṃskāra), or consciousness (vijñāna); it is to have no faith in the eye up to the mind (manas); it is to have no faith in visible objects up to mental phenomena (dharma); it is to have no faith in the eye-element up to the mind-consciousness element. It is to have no faith in the Perfection of Generosity (dānapāramitā), the Perfection of Ethics (śīlapāramitā), the Perfection of Patience (kṣāntipāramitā), the Perfection of Diligence (vīryapāramitā), or the Perfection of Meditative Concentration (dhyānapāramitā). It is to have no faith in internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the existence and non-existence of phenomena; it is to have no faith in the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path (ārya-mārga); it is to have no faith in the ten powers of a Buddha (daśabala) up to the eighteen exclusive attributes of a Buddha. It is to have no faith in the fruit of a stream-enterer (srotāpanna-phala), the fruit of a once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin-phala), the fruit of a non-returner (anāgāmin-phala), the fruit of an arhat (arhat-phala), or the path of a solitary buddha (pratyekabuddha-mārga); it is to have no faith in the bodhisattva path (bodhisattva-mārga); it is to have no faith in unsurpassed, perfect awakening (anuttara-samyaksambodhi) up to the omniscience of all aspects (sarva-ākārajñatā)."

source: 佛告阿濕波誓：「若沙門、婆羅門三昧堅固，三昧平等，若不得入彼三昧，不應作念：『我於三昧退減。』若復聖弟子不見色是我、異我、相在，不見受、想、行、識是我、異我、相在，但當作是覺知：『貪欲永盡無餘，瞋恚、愚癡永盡無餘。』貪、恚、癡永盡無餘已，一切漏盡，無漏心解脫、慧解脫，現法自知作證：『我生已盡，梵行已立，所作已作，自知不受後有。』」
A: The Buddha said to Aśvajit: "If a renunciant (śramaṇa) or a brahmin (brāhmaṇa) has a firm concentration (samādhi) and an equanimous concentration, yet cannot enter that concentration, they should not think: 'I have regressed in concentration.' If, furthermore, a noble disciple (ārya-śrāvaka) does not view bodily form as 'this is mine,' 'this is different from me,' or 'this is contained within me,' and does not view feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness as 'this is mine,' 'this is different from me,' or 'this is contained within me,' they should simply be aware: 'Greed (kāma-rāga) is forever ended without remainder; hatred and delusion are forever ended without remainder.' Once greed, hatred, and delusion are forever ended without remainder, all influxes (āsrava) are ended, and they attain an influx-free (anāsrava) liberation of the mind (cetas-vimukti) and liberation by wisdom (prajñā-vimukti), personally knowing and realizing here and now: 'Birth for me has been eradicated, the holy life (brahmacarya) has been established, what had to be done (kṛtya) has been done, and I myself know that there will be no receiving of further existence.'"
B: The Buddha said to Aśvajit: "If a renunciant (śramaṇa) or a priest (brāhmaṇa) has firm concentration (samādhi) and balanced concentration, yet cannot enter that concentration, they should not think: 'I have regressed in my concentration.' Furthermore, if a noble disciple does not view bodily form (rūpa) as 'this is mine,' 'this is different from me,' or 'this is within me,' and does not view feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), mental formations (saṃskāra), or consciousness (vijñāna) as 'this is mine,' 'this is different from me,' or 'this is within me,' they should simply be aware: 'Greed (kāma-rāga) is forever ended without remainder; hatred and delusion are forever ended without remainder.' Once greed, hatred, and delusion are forever ended without remainder, all influxes (āsrava) are ended, and they attain the influx-free liberation of the mind (ceto-vimukti) and liberation by wisdom (prajñā-vimukti). Here and now (dṛṣṭadharma), they personally know and realize: 'Birth for me has been eradicated, the holy life (brahmacarya) has been established, what had to be done (kṛtya) has been done, and I myself know that there will be no receiving of further existence (punarbhava).'"
